metadata.title: The reading rainbow of young multilingual learners: Reading comprehension in the majority (Spanish), regional (Basque) and foreign (English) language

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a convenience sample of 199 primary-school learners from five state-funded schools in the same Spanish city, with inclusion based on English-start timing and restrictions on English use at home and recent residence in English-speaking countries. The paper does not report the use of complex survey weights or any ILSA-style sampling weights, and it does not mention replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife). Because the analysis is based on small, school-based samples and standard regression/t-test procedures rather than ILSA microdata estimation, no weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is specified. The main preprocessing described is coding of questionnaire/test scores and splitting participants into HI vs LI groups and, for some analyses, quartiles by NVI; no missing-data imputation strategy is reported.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variables are raw scores from researcher-administered reading comprehension tests (English, Spanish, and Basque) and not ILSA PV-based achievement scales. Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper does not describe any exclusion rules beyond the initial participant eligibility criteria, nor does it report how missing questionnaire/test responses were treated. Given the study’s small sample and multiple instruments, this omission limits reproducibility regarding potential bias from any unreported missingness.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample comprised 199 young EFL learners from five state-funded schools in one Spanish city. Inclusion required: (i) learners began learning English in school no later than the first year of primary; (ii) learners did not use English at home with parents/siblings/friends; and (iii) learners had not spent more than two weeks in an English-speaking country. Participants were then assigned to high-intensity (HI; n=118) vs low-intensity (LI; n=81) tracks based on the intensity of CLIL exposure in school; LI learners were in Basque-immersion schools and were assessed in Basque in addition to Spanish. Additional classification for ER involved a supplementary extracurricular English questionnaire, and some regression comparisons used NVI quartiles.

main_findings.dataset_used: Local study (Spain) — Primary reading comprehension tests (English, Spanish, Basque); HI vs LI tracks; no ILSA cycle
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using local Spain primary reading comprehension test data (English) for HI vs LI learners, the study leveraged Non-verbal intelligence (NVI), socioeconomic status (SES), and extramural reading (ER) to predict English reading comprehension, finding that HI learners scored higher than LI learners and that NVI was the consistent significant predictor (with SES also significant only in the HI group) while ER showed no measurable effect. This indicates that strengthening cognitive readiness (e.g., supporting domain-general reasoning) may be more actionable than increasing reported out-of-school reading time for improving early English reading in high-intensity CLIL contexts, though causality cannot be inferred from this cross-sectional design.

main_findings.dataset_used: Local study (Spain) — Primary reading comprehension tests (Spanish, Basque); LI group only; no ILSA cycle
main_findings.performance_metrics: LI group language comparison (Spanish vs Basque): Spanish mean 6.20 vs Basque mean 4.78; t(80)=29.92 (reported); p<.001; Cohen’s d=0.612. Multiple regression (LI, Basque): R2=0.079, F=2.210, p=.094; NVI β=0.279 (p=.014) significant, SES β=-0.079 (p=.485) not significant, ER β=0.060 (p=.596) not significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using local Spain primary reading comprehension test data (Basque within the LI group), the study leveraged Non-verbal intelligence (NVI), socioeconomic status (SES), and extramural reading (ER) to predict Basque reading comprehension, finding that Basque scores were significantly lower than Spanish scores and that NVI was the only significant predictor in the Basque model while SES and ER were not. This indicates that early Basque immersion learners may require targeted support for cognitive/reading readiness to close the minority-language comprehension gap, while simply increasing reported extramural reading time is unlikely to be sufficient.

main_findings.dataset_used: Local study (Spain) — Primary reading comprehension tests (Spanish); HI vs LI tracks; no ILSA cycle
main_findings.performance_metrics: Group difference (HI vs LI): mean 6.27 vs 6.20; t(197)=0.283; p=.348; Cohen’s d=0.135. Multiple regression (HI, Spanish): R2=0.241, F=12.092, p<.001; NVI β=0.412 (p<.001), SES β=0.240 (p=.005), ER β=-0.044 (p=.606). Multiple regression (LI, Spanish): R2=0.099, F=2.807, p=.045; NVI β=0.303 (p=.007), SES β=-0.008 (p=.941), ER β=-0.082 (p=.451).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using local Spain primary reading comprehension test data (Spanish) for HI vs LI learners, the study leveraged Non-verbal intelligence (NVI), socioeconomic status (SES), and extramural reading (ER) to predict Spanish reading comprehension, finding no significant HI–LI difference in Spanish scores but showing that NVI was a significant predictor in both groups (with SES significant only in the HI group) and ER showing no significant effect. This indicates that minority-language immersion does not appear to harm majority-language reading at this age, but cognitive readiness remains a key lever for improving reading outcomes regardless of instructional intensity.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzed 199 primary-school learners in Spain from five state-funded schools, comparing high-intensity CLIL exposure (HI; n=118) versus low-intensity Basque-immersion contexts (LI; n=81). Reading comprehension was measured with online tests in English and Spanish for all learners, and in Basque for LI learners; NVI was measured with Raven’s Progressive Matrices, SES via a regional SES questionnaire, and ER via self-reported out-of-school reading time. The key quantitative results show higher English reading in HI than LI (p=.001; d=.548), lower Basque than Spanish in LI (p<.001; d=.612), and strong cross-language correlations. Multiple regression indicated NVI as the most consistent predictor of reading scores (e.g., English HI: R2=.180; β_NVI=.344, p<.001), SES as a secondary predictor mainly in HI, and ER as non-significant across models. Limitations include the absence of PVs/weights (not ILSA microdata), no reported missing-data handling, and no causal identification strategy.
